title: Missions and empire, honestly
hook: missionaries brought schools and hospitals, and sometimes empire's arrogance; local Christians often led the growth
carry: the gospel is not an empire

segments.voice: Yesterday: William Carey, the shoemaker who taught himself languages and sailed for India. Your line was expect great things.

A ship comes into harbor. On board, a missionary with a trunk of Bibles, and on the same ship, a soldier, a trader and a government clerk. They step onto the dock together. From the shore, it can be hard to tell who works for whom. In the same years that European empires spread across Africa and Asia, missionaries went too. It's a hard chapter in the Christian story. Today, the honest version.

Start with the good; it was real. Missionaries opened schools, ran hospitals and clinics, learned local languages with real love, and translated the Bible into languages that had never seen it in print. Some stood up to traders and officials for the people they lived among. Now the hard part. Some carried the empire's pride. They treated local cultures as worthless, wanted converts to dress and sing and name their children like Europeans, and kept local Christians out of leadership for a long time. Some leaned on colonial power. Some Christians today, in churches at both ends, say this openly. The part that's easy to miss: the faith grew through local people whose names never made it home to Europe. Catechists, evangelists, Bible women, translators. In West Africa a Liberian preacher, William Wadé Harris, walked the coast in a white robe with a cross and a Bible, and tradition says crowds were baptized after hearing him. In India, Pandita Ramabai, a scholar of Sanskrit, became a Christian and opened homes for widows and girls. They weren't stand-ins for foreigners. They led. Underneath it all is a line Jesus spoke, in the King James Bible: "Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them. But it shall not be so among you." And before Pilate: "My kingdom is not of this world." Some Christians looking back return to those words: the gospel came with an empire, but was never meant to be one. Look back over the week: Richard Allen walking out, Equiano telling his story, Wilberforce, Sunday schools, Carey. Again and again, change came from people at the edges, and from those who listened.
screen: `IT SHALL NOT BE SO AMONG YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people usually left out: the translator, the evangelist who walked, the woman who taught the first class. Say one name quietly, Harris, Ramabai, or a pastor in your own town. If you pray, give thanks for them; if you don't, let the name sit beside the famous ones, just as large.
Ramabai. A Sanskrit scholar in India who became a Christian and opened homes for widows and girls, leading her own mission rather than following a foreign one.
Your line: the gospel is not an empire. Helping someone never has to mean making them like you. Day nine hundred seventeen, done.

howItsDone: Churches that began through missions, and churches that sent missionaries, sometimes look back on this history together, honoring local founders and naming the harm done alongside the good.

options: wait quietly until they hand it over.
start preaching yourself, in your own language.

fork.reveal: on the West African coast, local people did exactly that. William Wadé Harris walked the coast preaching, and tradition says crowds were baptized after hearing him.

chat.says: Weren't Christian missionaries back then just part of the empires?
options: Some leaned on empire, but local leaders like Ramabai led much of the growth.
No, missionaries never had anything to do with the empires of their day.
Yes, and churches only grew where foreign missionaries stayed in charge.
chat.meaning: The lesson names both: some missionaries leaned on colonial power, yet local Christians like Harris and Ramabai led much of the growth.
